extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, advocates, funders, and practitioners interested in technology and society
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Data & Society's research tracks, cross-cutting themes, projects, and approach; emphasizes empirical, participatory, and justice-oriented investigations of technology's social impacts. Useful as guidance for designing, evaluating, or aligning research and program work in sociotechnical domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous and relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Data & Society researchers produce rigorous and relevant evidence to ground and inform public debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should be both methodologically rigorous and relevant to public debates — providing evidence that meaningfully informs discussions about technology and society rather than merely amplifying hype or fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor Futures (research track)
rubrics_metrics.description: We interrogate how technology is disrupting, destabilizing, and transforming many aspects of work and employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research in this track should examine technological impacts on labor systems, worker experiences, employment patterns, and power dynamics, prioritizing empirical investigation of disruption and transformation in work.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI on the Ground (research track)
rubrics_metrics.description: We use social science to develop robust analyses of AI systems; effectively assess the impact of AI systems; and inform future design, use, and governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should apply social-science methods to produce robust, context-sensitive analyses of deployed AI, assess their real-world impacts, and generate recommendations for design and governance that are grounded in evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthy Infrastructures (research track)
rubrics_metrics.description: We explore how diverse sets of communities shape their collective responses to top-down technological solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should center community perspectives and practices, studying how different communities adapt to, resist, or reconfigure infrastructures imposed from above, with attention to trust, resilience, and local governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate, Technology, and Justice (research track)
rubrics_metrics.description: With a focus on people and communities, our research explores the full spectrum of environmental concerns connected to technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should link technological systems to environmental outcomes and justice concerns, prioritizing community-centered approaches to understand socio-environmental impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation, Agency, and Algorithmic Accountability (cross-cutting theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: We explore methods, institutions, and mandates that aim to empower communities to shape the systems that impact their lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects under this theme should evaluate and develop mechanisms (methods, institutional arrangements, policies) that increase participation and agency, and enable accountability for algorithmic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technologies of Health and Care (cross-cutting theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: We examine the power dynamics embedded in how health data and technology are designed, used, and applied in care settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should interrogate design, governance, and deployment of health technologies and data practices, emphasizing power, equity, and effects on care relationships and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic Impact Methods (AIMLab project standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIMLab works to develop methodologies for conducting empirical, participatory algorithmic impact assessments to support the governance of artificial intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological work should be empirical and participatory, producing practical approaches for algorithmic impact assessment that can be used by communities and governance actors to evaluate and regulate AI systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame-breaking, empirically grounded approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates about the societal influence of data and automation cannot meaningfully happen without an evidence base, drawn from empirical research, that challenges the hype and fear surrounding sociotechnical systems. At Data & Society, we pursue frame-breaking research questions informed by the realities of those who may be adversely affected by the integration and implementation of these technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should be empirical, challenge prevailing frames or assumptions, ask disruptive or 'frame-breaking' questions, and be informed by the lived realities of communities likely to be harmed — centering those perspectives in question formulation and interpretation.
